subtype: Team hit by a late finisher [Receiver]
passage: The class six report cards had to reach the principal by Friday morning. In the school staffroom, Charu, the class teacher, had every subject's marks in her spreadsheet except science. Vikas had promised them on Tuesday. On Wednesday he said, "Tonight, pakka." On Thursday at 4:15 a message arrived: "Sorry, sorry, sending now." Charu stayed on as the cleaners switched off the corridor lights. She entered thirty-eight science scores, redid the averages, found that the rank list had shifted, and rewrote four remarks she had already printed. At 8:10 she texted her sister: "Can't make dinner. Save me some." Walking to the bus stop, her shoulders ached. Vikas would sleep fine tonight, she thought, and felt mean for thinking it, and then just tired.

qa.q: How many science scores did Charu enter on Thursday evening?
qa.a: She entered thirty-eight science scores.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling on the walk to the bus stop?
qa.a: She felt resentful that Vikas would sleep fine, then guilty for the thought, and above all exhausted after the long evening.

qa.q: What could Vikas have done on Tuesday that would have helped Charu?
qa.a: He could have told her on Tuesday that the marks were running late and given a real date, so she could plan her evening instead of losing it at the last minute.

qa.q: How might Vikas see the delay differently from Charu?
qa.a: Vikas may see it as a small slip covered by an apology, without seeing the four hours, the redone rank list and the missed dinner it cost her.

grounding: Shows a colleague who has to squeeze her own work and stay late because someone else's input arrived after the promised date.

subtype: Warning early when a deadline will slip [Response]
passage: "You know what I learned this year, Simran? Bad news goes sour if you keep it. I'm Vishal, I run the finishing bench at my uncle's furniture workshop in Jaipur. In March we promised Mrs Rathore a dining set by the 15th; her son's engagement lunch was on the 17th. On the 2nd, the timber supplier said the teak would be ten days late. The old me would have kept quiet and hoped. Instead I called her that same afternoon. I said, 'The table can't be ready by the 15th. The realistic date is the 24th. Option one: we deliver the six chairs on the 14th and lend you our long folding table. Option two: we use the sheesham we have in stock and keep the date.' She was annoyed for about two minutes, then chose the chairs. Later she sent us two more orders, and she told my uncle, 'At least he told me in time.'"

qa.q: When was Mrs Rathore's son's engagement lunch?
qa.a: On the 17th.

qa.q: What might Vishal have felt before making that call, and what hints at it?
qa.a: Vishal was probably nervous about her reaction; saying the old self would have kept quiet and hoped shows how tempting silence felt.

qa.q: What made Vishal's call useful rather than just bad news?
qa.a: He called on the same day he knew, gave a realistic new date, and offered two options, so Mrs Rathore could still plan the lunch.

qa.q: What would change for Mrs Rathore if she had heard about the delay only on the 14th?
qa.a: She would have had no time to arrange a table for the lunch and would likely have felt let down and betrayed, and the extra orders probably would not have come.

grounding: Illustrates a worker who warns the customer as soon as a date looks unsafe, with a new realistic date and options, and keeps her trust.

subtype: Exams, tuition, family and friends together [Actor]
passage: Looking back, I can see it clearly, but at the time I just thought everyone was being annoying. That was the week of my pre-board maths paper. Coaching ran from five to eight. My cousin's nikah was on Saturday, and Ammi needed me to fetch chairs from the tent house. Yash kept messaging about his birthday football match. Nobody asked me how I was, and I didn't say. Instead, when my little brother asked me to help with his kite, I shouted so loudly that he cried. I slammed the door on Ammi over a cup of tea. On Thursday Yash said, "Irfan, you've been biting everyone's head off." That was the first time I thought: oh. I'm not angry at them. I'm stretched too thin.

qa.q: When did Irfan's coaching run that week?
qa.a: Coaching ran from five to eight.

qa.q: What was Irfan really feeling underneath the shouting?
qa.a: Irfan was overwhelmed and pulled apart by the paper, coaching, the nikah and Yash's match; the irritation was the overload showing, not real anger at the family.

qa.q: What small step could have helped Irfan earlier in that week?
qa.a: Irfan could have told Ammi and Yash how packed the week was and asked for one thing to move, such as someone else fetching the chairs.

qa.q: What was it like for Irfan's little brother when he asked about the kite?
qa.a: He asked for a small, happy thing and got shouted at, so he was hurt and confused and cried, not knowing what he had done.

grounding: Shows a teenager juggling exams, coaching, a family wedding and friends whose overload first comes out as snapping at family.

passage:
Wednesday, 11 pm
Said yes to three more things today. Salma asked if I'd proofread her internship cover letter (sure!). The dance society needs someone to make costumes for the fest (me, obviously). And a senior offered me a paid tutoring slot on Saturdays, and I couldn't turn it down. What if nobody asks again?
Full list now: dance, drama club, NSS on Sundays, tutoring, Salma's letter, and the quiz club I joined because everyone I like is in it.
Then the statistics test results came out. 11 out of 30. I haven't opened the textbook since the second week. Dr Menon wrote "See me" on the sheet.
I sat on the hostel stairs and felt sick. Every single yes felt right at the time. Saying no feels like letting someone down, or missing the one night that matters.
Tomorrow: see Dr Menon. And maybe tell the dance people I can't do costumes.
Yamini

qa.q: What did Yamini score on the statistics test?
qa.a: 11 out of 30.

qa.q: Why does Yamini keep saying yes to everything?
qa.a: Yamini is afraid of letting people down and worried about missing out, so each yes feels right in the moment even as the core work slides.

qa.q: What would you advise Yamini to do first?
qa.a: Keep the plan to see Dr Menon, hand back one commitment such as the costumes, and set aside fixed statistics time before adding anything new.

qa.q: How might Salma feel if she knew what the week looked like?
qa.a: Salma would likely be grateful for the proofreading but also uneasy, and might rather wait for it than have Yamini fall further behind.

grounding: Shows a student who takes on every club, favour and offer out of fear of disappointing people and missing out, then falls behind on core coursework.

passage:
Siddharth: hey, you ok? you sighed about twenty times at robotics practice 😅
Pankaj: sorry. just a lot
Siddharth: you skipped mess lunch again too. third day
Pankaj: no time. lab record due fri, TA duty, cousin's wedding calls every night
Pankaj: and I forgot to order the motor driver for the robot. that one's on me
Siddharth: no lecture, promise. what can I take off your plate?
Pankaj: ...seriously?
Siddharth: I'll place the parts order tonight. and I'll bring you a plate from the mess tomorrow at 1
Pankaj: that would honestly save me
Pankaj: the order list is in the team folder
Siddharth: found it. order placed. go sleep 🙂
Pankaj: thanks yaar 🙏
Siddharth: tomorrow, 1 pm, lab door. don't hide

qa.q: How many days in a row had Pankaj skipped mess lunch?
qa.a: Three days; Siddharth says it is the third day.

qa.q: What does Siddharth's "no lecture, promise" suggest about how Siddharth feels?
qa.a: Siddharth is concerned and caring, and wants Pankaj to feel safe admitting the slip instead of feeling judged.

qa.q: Why was asking what to take off Pankaj's plate more useful than advice?
qa.a: It removed real work, the parts order and the lunch trip, instead of adding one more thing for Pankaj to think about.

qa.q: What is it like for Pankaj to get this offer?
qa.a: Pankaj is surprised at first ("...seriously?") and then relieved, since one task is lifted and someone has noticed without scolding.

grounding: Illustrates a peer who notices sighing, a missed detail and skipped lunches and helps by taking tasks off the other person's plate rather than giving advice.

subtype: Work, family and personal duties colliding [Actor]
passage:
Team lead's note, Friday. Samir.
For three weeks Tanvir has left at six sharp on Tuesdays and Thursdays to drive his parents to his father's physiotherapy, then logged in again at ten at night. On Wednesday he stayed back after stand-up and told me his mother also wants him home every Sunday, and his fiancée has stopped asking when they will look at wedding venues. He said, "Whatever I pick, somebody's let down. Some days I'm angry at all of them, and then I feel terrible for being angry at my own parents." He rubbed his eyes the whole time.
I didn't try to solve his family. I moved the client review from Thursday to Monday and told him late-night logins are not expected. I also said both feelings can be true at once. I'll check in again next Friday.

qa.q: On which days did Tanvir leave at six?
qa.a: On Tuesdays and Thursdays.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Tanvir describe?
qa.a: He feels guilty whichever duty he neglects, resentful towards everyone pulling at him, and then ashamed of that anger towards his own parents.

qa.q: Which of Samir's steps helped most, and why?
qa.a: Moving the client review and saying late logins are not expected eased real pressure, and saying both feelings can be true lets Tanvir stop fighting himself.

qa.q: How might Tanvir's fiancée be feeling, given that she has stopped asking about venues?
qa.a: She may feel pushed to the bottom of the list and quietly hurt or resigned, as if asking again would only add to his load.

grounding: Shows a young professional torn between a demanding job, his parents' needs and his own relationship, feeling guilt and resentment at once.

passage:
Naveen,
I'm writing this because last night's fight about the dishes was not about the dishes, and I shouted instead of saying it properly.
Since your promotion in June, you're here but not here. At Ma's birthday dinner you spent dessert on the terrace on a call. On our Saturday walks you walk a step behind, typing. When I told you my article got accepted, you said "wow, great" without looking up, and an hour later asked what article.
I kept quiet for months because I know the job matters, and I am proud of you. But slowly I've started to feel like the last item on your list, after the laptop, after the team, after sleep.
I don't want you to quit. I want one evening a week when the phone lives in the drawer, and I want you to ask about my day and wait for the answer.
Can we talk tonight, without the dishes?
Bidisha

qa.q: What did Naveen say on hearing the article had been accepted?
qa.a: "Wow, great", without looking up, and an hour later asked what article.

qa.q: What has Bidisha been feeling during the months of keeping quiet?
qa.a: Bidisha has felt hurt and lonely, like the last item on Naveen's list, while still being proud of the promotion.

qa.q: What does the letter do that last night's fight did not?
qa.a: It names the real problem with specific moments and asks for one clear change, a phone-free evening and real listening, instead of shouting about dishes.

qa.q: What might it be like for Naveen to read this letter?
qa.a: Naveen may feel surprised and guilty, perhaps a little defensive, realising the distance was felt so strongly while Naveen thought things were fine.

grounding: Shows a partner who has quietly felt last on the list behind a busy worker's job until it spilled out as an argument.

passage: On Sunday evening in her Bengaluru flat, Jahnavi tore a page from a notebook and wrote down everything she had promised: the manuscript edit due to the publisher on Thursday, packing for the move, Kannada class twice a week, and Darshan's pitch deck, which she had said she'd polish by Friday. Seeing it all on one page made her stomach drop. Then she numbered it. Manuscript first. Then she sent three messages. To Darshan: "I can't do the deck by Friday. I can give it a proper look next Wednesday. Is that okay, or should you ask someone else?" To her Kannada teacher: "Skipping two weeks, back on the 20th." To the landlord: "Can the move shift by a week?" On Monday she worked only on the manuscript, phone face-down until lunch. It went out on Thursday morning. Darshan had replied within an hour: "Thanks for telling me. Wednesday works."

qa.q: What did Jahnavi put first on the numbered list?
qa.a: The manuscript edit due to the publisher on Thursday.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel when she saw everything on one page?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed, her stomach dropped, and she became calmer once the list was numbered and the messages were sent.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Telling Darshan, the teacher and the landlord what would slip, then doing one thing at a time, let her finish the manuscript without quietly failing the others.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel getting the message on Sunday rather than a missed Friday?
qa.a: Darshan is relieved and grateful to know early, with time to choose between waiting and asking someone else.

grounding: Illustrates listing all commitments, telling the right people what will be delayed and working through them one at a time.

subtype: Child too shy or proud to ask [Actor]
passage: I'm Pooja. In class four we started long division, and on the first day I got lost at the step where you bring the next number down. Miss Thomas asked, "Everyone clear?" Lokesh, next to me, was already on sum three. I nodded. My ears went hot. I thought if I asked, the whole row would know I was the only one who didn't get it. The next day I copied the steps from the board without understanding them. By Friday there was a worksheet of ten sums, and I got two right. I hid it inside my atlas. Now I think the nod was the mistake. Every day I stayed quiet, the part I didn't understand got bigger.

qa.q: At which step of long division did Pooja get lost?
qa.a: At the step where you bring the next number down.

qa.q: Why did Pooja nod when Miss Thomas asked if everyone was clear?
qa.a: Pooja felt embarrassed and afraid of looking like the only one who didn't get it, which the hot ears show.

qa.q: What could Pooja try next time something is confusing?
qa.a: Pooja could ask Miss Thomas quietly after class, or write the question on a slip of paper, so nobody in the row has to hear.

qa.q: What would change if Pooja had asked on the very first day?
qa.a: The confusion about one step could have been cleared in minutes, before it grew into a worksheet with only two right and a hidden sheet.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild who stays silent over a confusing step for fear of looking stupid, so the confusion quietly grows.

passage:
Thursday
Five weeks now of pretending I understand trigonometry identities. Today Mrs Pillai asked the class, "Who wants to come to the doubt session at lunch?" Three people raised their hands. Jeevan didn't need to, obviously; Jeevan finishes the worksheet before she's done writing it on the board. I kept my hands flat on the desk. If I go, everyone will know the "bright one" can't do sin and cos.
So instead I spent two hours tonight on videos and got more confused. Got 9 out of 25 on the class test. Mum saw it and asked why I never ask for help. I said I'm figuring it out.
Am I, though? Five weeks. If I'd gone in week one it would probably be sorted by now.
Maybe tomorrow at lunch. Maybe.
Trisha

qa.q: How many people raised their hands for the doubt session?
qa.a: Three people raised their hands.

qa.q: Why did Trisha keep both hands flat on the desk?
qa.a: Trisha was afraid of being judged and too proud to let the class see the "bright one" struggling, so staying still felt safer.

qa.q: What small step could Trisha take tomorrow?
qa.a: Go to the lunch doubt session with one written question, or ask Mrs Pillai privately before class, so the first ask is short and less public.

qa.q: If you were Mrs Pillai, what would you want Trisha to know?
qa.a: That the doubt session is exactly for this, that asking is not failing, and that five weeks of struggle could have been a few minutes of help.

grounding: Shows a teenager who struggles alone for weeks because asking the teacher in front of capable peers feels like admitting failure.
